content: Option 1 involves using the Xpert Ultra test as the primary diagnostic tool for all individuals who screen positive for tuberculosis (TB). If the Xpert Ultra test yields a positive result, confirmatory testing is conducted using the Mycobacteria Growth Indicator Tube (MGIT) culture method. This approach significantly reduces the need for culture testing, typically requiring fewer than 300 tests, which is less than 10% of the workload required for Option 2. This reduction addresses the suboptimal specificity of the Xpert Ultra test, which can result in a high rate of false-positive results in prevalence surveys. However, it is crucial to ensure high-quality liquid culture testing to avoid false-negative culture results, which could misclassify some Xpert-positive individuals as false positives. During the pilot and early phases of a survey, it is recommended to compare culture and Xpert Ultra results to assess the performance of culture testing and implement corrective actions if necessary. The main disadvantages of Option 1 include lower sensitivity compared to Option 2, logistical challenges in organizing Xpert Ultra testing to ensure timely results, and difficulties in comparing results with previous surveys that used different diagnostic methods. Additionally, in some countries, establishing liquid culture capacity may be necessary. Option 2 relies on liquid culture testing (MGIT) of two separate sputum samples from all screen-positive individuals, complemented by an Xpert Ultra test to provide rapid results for clinical management. Liquid culture is considered the microbiological reference standard and, if performed well, detects the highest proportion of true positive TB cases in the community. However, ensuring high-quality culture testing in the context of a survey is challenging, as it requires efficient sample transportation, quality-assured culture performance, and sufficient laboratory capacity. This option is also more expensive than Option 1, as it involves both culture and rapid testing for all screen-positive individuals. Option 2 has limited experience in prevalence surveys, with only a few countries having implemented liquid culture testing for two samples from all screen-positive individuals. Additionally, logistical challenges arise from the need to collect and test multiple samples, and direct comparisons with previous surveys using different diagnostic methods are difficult. Despite these challenges, liquid culture testing remains the most reliable method for detecting TB cases when performed to a high standard.
